name: Expecting var to be block scoped
explanation: You treated var as if it belonged to the nearest block, the way let does. var belongs to the whole enclosing function (or the module), so it is still visible after the block or loop ends, and a var loop has one shared binding. Use let or const for a binding that lives only inside its block.

name: Reading a let or const before its declaration
explanation: You expected the name to be undefined, or to fall through to an outer variable, until its let or const line runs. The binding exists from the start of its block but sits in the temporal dead zone until the declaration runs, so reading it earlier throws a ReferenceError.

name: Confusing a const binding with a frozen value
explanation: You treated const as a rule about the value rather than the name. const fixes the binding, so the name cannot be reassigned, but the array or object it points to can still be changed with push or property assignment.

name: Thinking an inner declaration changes the outer variable
explanation: You treated a let inside a function or block as updating the variable of the same name outside. A new declaration creates a separate binding that shadows the outer one only in that scope; to change the outer variable, assign to it without let, const, or var.

name: Thinking a closure copies values
explanation: You treated the inner function as if it saved a snapshot of the variable when it was created. A closure keeps a live link to the variable itself, so it sees every later change and its own updates persist between calls.

name: Thinking every call shares one set of local variables
explanation: You treated a function's local variables as if every call shared them. Each call creates a fresh environment, so closures returned by two different calls each have their own variables.

name: Expecting a function to return its last expression
explanation: You expected the value of the last line to come back automatically. A function body in { } returns undefined unless a return statement runs; only an arrow function without braces, like (n) => n * 2, returns its expression.

name: Mixing up in-place and copying array methods
explanation: You assumed a method returned a new array when it changes the original, or the other way round. map, filter, slice, and spread build new arrays and leave the original alone, while push, splice, sort, and reverse change the array in place, and sort and reverse return that same array.

name: Expecting forEach to return a new array
explanation: You treated forEach like map. forEach calls your function for each element but always returns undefined, so use map to collect results or filter to keep some elements.

name: Expecting sort() to order numbers numerically
explanation: You assumed sort() compares numbers by size. With no compare function, sort converts the elements to strings and orders them character by character, so 10 comes before 9; pass (a, b) => a - b to sort numbers.

name: Removing elements while iterating over the array
explanation: You expected the loop to visit every original element even while splice removed some. for...of walks the array by index, and splice shifts later elements left, so the element that moves into the current index is skipped. Build a new array instead, for example with filter.

name: Treating the length as the last index
explanation: You treated xs.length as a valid index, or let the loop run while i <= xs.length. An array of length n has indexes 0 to n - 1, so xs[xs.length] is undefined and i <= xs.length runs one step too far; use i < xs.length and xs[xs.length - 1].

name: Thinking slice includes its end index
explanation: You expected slice(start, end) to include the element at end. slice copies from start up to but not including end, so slice(1, 3) returns two elements, the ones at indexes 1 and 2.

name: Counting a loop's runs from its bounds instead of its values
explanation: You counted the runs as the number in the condition, or forgot that <= adds a run. A loop from i = a while i < b runs b - a times, and while i <= b it runs b - a + 1 times; list the values i takes if unsure.

name: Thinking assignment or passing copies an object
explanation: You treated b = a, or passing a to a function, as making a copy. Both names hold a reference to the same object or array, so a change made through either one is visible through the other.

name: Thinking spread makes a deep copy
explanation: You expected { ...obj } or [...arr] to copy everything inside. Spread makes a new outer object but copies the references it holds, so nested arrays and objects are still shared with the original.

name: Thinking === compares objects by their contents
explanation: You expected two objects with the same properties to be equal. === on objects and arrays checks whether both sides are the same reference, so two separately created objects are never equal; compare their properties instead.

name: Thinking reassigning a parameter changes the caller's variable
explanation: You expected list = [] inside the function to replace the caller's array. Reassigning a parameter only points that local name somewhere new; to affect the caller, change the object itself, for example with push or by setting length.
